newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Labour sticks with Treasury numbers for policy.
newsitem.headline: NZ Labour sticks with Treasury numbers for policy.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party will "recrunch its numbers" for its policy programme using Treasury's pre-election economic and fiscal update, finance spokeamn Michael Cullen said on Friday.

On Friday the Reserve Bank released its economic projections which painted a more pessimistic picture than Treasury, but Cullen said the bank's projections did not dent Labour's confidence it could "implement programmes capable of addressing pressing social issues and building a strong economy".
He said using the Treasury figures would allow direct comparisons with the government's programme.

On Thursday Cullen said based on Treasury's figures Labour could meet its bottom line target of lowering net debt by two percent a year over the next three years if it won office in the October 12 general election.

Treasury's forecasts, released on Thursday, showed surpluses growing from $2.87 billion in the 1996/97 year to more than $6 billion by the turn of the century. It saw economic growth picking up from 2.5 percent in 1997 to 3.7 percent the following year.

But the Reserve Bank's projections assumed a lower growth track of two percent this year and 2.4 percent in 1997/98 producing surpluses declining from $2.25 billion in the 1996/97 year to $1.89 billion in the 1997/98 year.
"I don't think anyone should be surprised by the differences between the two forecasts," Cullen said.
"The Reserve Bank has consistently taken a less optimistic view of conditions than the Treasury."
He said Labour would be "continuing work on recrunching our numbers using the official (Treasury) forecasts".
But Labour's rivals on the left, the five party Alliance grouping, said the promises of Labour, and economic nationalists New Zealand First were "blown out of the water" by the RBNZ's projections.
Alliance leader Jim Anderton said Labour and New Zealand First were promising to "spend without raising revenue to pay for the promises".

Labour has said it will raise the tax on earnings above $60,000 from 33 percent to 39 percent and lower taxes for the low paid, but the Alliance has proposed a more progressive tax system that would raise more revenue.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, who is campaigning on the slogan "New Zealand for New Zealanders", said the RBNZ's projections "confirm that inflation has been fuelled by the construction boom based on immigration...and all New Zealanders must pay the cost".
He said the contrast between the RBNZ figures and Treasury's forecasts "require explanation".
"That contradiction suggests the usual Treasury party- political bias. The Reserve Bank forecast is more truthful. Vote National and they will deliver a deteriorating economy," Peters said.

Bank of New Zealand chief economist Tony Alexander said on Friday he would accord a greater degreee of independence and reliability to the RBNZ figures, but he was not surprised or concerned about the difference.
